The Shiva Linga at Rameshwaram

Stories from the Ramayana

The Shiva Linga at Rameshwaram

One line in Valmiki — and a temple in the later tellings

In everyday English — Yuddha Kanda 123.19 and later tradition

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it aloud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home.

This book is to be read in two ways. First, what is really written in Valmiki's Ramayana — that is very short, only one line. Then what the later tellings say — that is very beloved, and millions of people hold it true. Hear the two separately — and wherever it says “the later telling”, understand that it is not a line from Valmiki, but a story told afterwards.

The yellow boxes hold the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little as you read them — Rama calm, Hanuman devoted, Sita gentle.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listeners speak.

The Valmiki line of this book is Yuddha Kanda, sarga 123, verse 19. The later telling is told in the Adhyatma Ramayana, the Shiva Purana, the Skanda Purana and the Ramcharitmanas. Anything else you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — son of Dasharatha, tall and calm, warm dark-brown skin, wearing his upper cloth, bow in hand. In this book he worships Shiva on the shore of the sea — in the later telling.

Sita — daughter of Janaka, gentle face, large dark eyes, long black braid with small white jasmine flowers, light saree. She is returning home with Rama.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother, a little lighter in complexion, bow in hand. He is with Rama.

Hanuman — son of the Wind, a powerful vanara, light golden-brown fur, long tail, gentle devoted face, saffron dhoti. In the later telling he brings a linga from Kailasa.

Shiva — Mahadeva. In this book he is worshipped in the form of the Shiva linga — no statue, only the linga.

Sugriva and Vibhishana — king of the vanaras and the new king of Lanka. They are returning with Rama.

1 · On the Way Home — One Line · · ON THE WAY HOME — ONE LINE

The war was over. Ravana was dead. Sita had come back. Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, Sugriva and Vibhishana were flying home to Ayodhya in the Pushpaka vimana.

On the way the vimana passed over the shore of the sea — the very place from where the bridge had been built. Rama showed it to Sita — and said —

Rama said: “Sita, look — this is the shore where Mahadeva formerly bestowed his grace on me.”

That is all. In Valmiki's Ramayana nothing more is written about it. It is not written that Rama made a Shiva linga there, nor that Hanuman went to Kailasa, nor how the worship happened.

This is one line — sarga 123 of the Yuddha Kanda, verse 19. And there is a question about this one line too — some people say that here “Mahadeva” does not mean Shiva, but Sagara, the ocean — the ocean bestowed its grace on Rama.

So in this book we tell this line just as it is — without adding anything. And the story that was told afterwards, we tell separately — calling it “the later telling”.

Pause and think — Why did Valmiki write only one line? Can one line sometimes be very great? And when one line can have two meanings — Shiva or the ocean — should both be heard?

2 · What Valmiki Does Not Say · · WHAT VALMIKI DOES NOT SAY

Now know this — so that there is no confusion.

In Valmiki's Ramayana it is not written that Rama made a Shiva linga of sand on the shore of the sea. It is not written that Hanuman went to Kailasa or Kashi to fetch a linga. It is not written that there are two lingas there.

In Valmiki there is no story of worship before the building of the bridge. The bridge was built — by speaking with Varuna and the ocean, with arrows, with stones — but there is no story of installing a Shiva linga there.

This is not something to hide — it is something to tell. Because the story told afterwards is also very beloved — and it is just as good to hear it, as long as we know that it is a later telling.

So now hear — the later telling.

Pause and think — Is it necessary to know which part is in Valmiki and which part is in the later telling? And when a story was told afterwards, does it become less beloved — or does it stay just as beloved?

3 · The Later Telling — The Sand Linga · · THE LATER TELLING — THE SAND LINGA

The later telling — told in the Adhyatma Ramayana, the Shiva Purana, the Skanda Purana and the Ramcharitmanas — goes like this.

Rama stood on the shore of the sea — before him the vast ocean, and across it, Lanka. Before building the bridge, Rama thought — first Shiva should be worshipped.

Rama took the sand of the shore — and with his own hands made a Shiva linga. Then he worshipped it — with flowers, with water, and with the peace of his heart.

It is said that Shiva, pleased with Rama's worship, blessed him — and said that whoever comes here and worships this linga will find peace.

Rama worshipped — and then the building of the bridge began.

Pause and think — In the later telling, why did Rama worship before the bridge? Is stopping to worship before a great task also a kind of preparation? And Rama made the linga from sand — is a linga of sand just as holy as one of stone?

4 · The Later Telling — Hanuman's Journey · · THE LATER TELLING — HANUMAN'S JOURNEY

The later telling goes on to say — Rama thought that another Shiva linga should also be brought for the worship — from Kailasa, the abode of Shiva.

Rama said to Hanuman — “Hanuman, you go to Kailasa — and bring a Shiva linga from there.”

Hanuman flew away — through the sky, above the clouds, towards the Himalayas. He reached Kailasa — and started back with a Shiva linga.

But Hanuman was delayed on his way back. The time for worship was passing — and Rama made a linga of sand and finished the worship.

When Hanuman returned — carrying the linga — he saw that the worship was already done. He grew sad.

Rama said — “Hanuman, do not be sad. The linga you brought will also stay here — and it will be worshipped first, and then the one I made. Both will be worshipped — both will be honoured.”

In some tellings it is said that Hanuman brought the linga from Kashi — not from Kailasa. Both kinds of tellings are told — and in this book we name both, so that there is no confusion.

Pause and think — Why was Hanuman delayed? Can being late sometimes be good — because it led to two lingas being worshipped? And Rama said — your linga will be worshipped first. Was that love for Hanuman — or justice?

5 · The Later Telling — Two Lingas · · THE LATER TELLING — TWO LINGAS

The later telling says — at Rameshwaram today there are two Shiva lingas.

One is the one Rama made with his own hands from sand — it is called Ramanatha, the Lord of Rama. The other is the one Hanuman brought from Kailasa — or Kashi — it is called Vishwanatha.

And it is said that the order of worship here is the same as Rama fixed — first Vishwanatha is worshipped, then Ramanatha.

This story is not in Valmiki — it is in the later tellings. But millions of people hold it true — and go to Rameshwaram to worship both lingas.

Pause and think — Why are there two Shiva lingas — one made by Rama, one brought by Hanuman? Does worshipping both show that what a devotee brings is just as holy as what the Lord makes?

6 · The Later Telling — Towards the Bridge and the War · · THE LATER TELLING — TOWARDS THE BRIDGE AND THE WAR

In the later telling — after the worship, Rama built the bridge — the vanaras lifted stones, Nala and Nila built the causeway, and the army crossed the sea to Lanka.

Then the war happened — and Ravana was killed. Sita returned. And Rama flew back to Ayodhya in the Pushpaka vimana — passing over the same shore where he had worshipped.

And on the way home Rama said to Sita — “This is the shore where Mahadeva bestowed his grace on me.”

Here the later telling and Valmiki's line meet — the same shore, the same words.

Pause and think — In the later telling the worship happened before the bridge — and in Valmiki there is only the line spoken on the way home. Is it good to hear both together — or separately?

7 · Rameshwaram Today · · RAMESHWARAM TODAY

Today at Rameshwaram there is a great temple — the Ramanathaswamy Temple. It stands on an island on the sea-coast of Tamil Nadu.

It is said that this is the shore where Rama worshipped — and from where the bridge was built. This is held by tradition — it is not proven by archaeology, but millions of people hold it true.

In the temple there are both Shiva lingas — Ramanatha and Vishwanatha. The temple has long, long corridors, and sacred tanks — the theerthams — in which people bathe and then worship.

Every year millions of people go to Rameshwaram — to worship Rama, to worship Shiva, and to see the sea.

And when they come out of the temple and stand on the shore of the sea, they see the same thing Rama saw — the vast ocean, and the road going across towards Lanka.

So the story of Rameshwaram, which began with one line — and grew through the later tellings — is alive even today.

Pause and think — Rameshwaram is still a living temple today — millions of people go there. Is a story staying alive its greatest truth? And if you ever go to Rameshwaram, would you want to see that shore?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

In this book we heard two things separately — one, Valmiki's one line: “This is the shore where Mahadeva bestowed his grace on me.” Two, the later telling: the sand linga, Hanuman's journey, the two lingas, and Rameshwaram today.

Knowing the two apart is necessary — but hearing both is just as good. One line is true — and the later telling is also true in the hearts of millions of people.

Ask your listeners:

1. Why did Valmiki write only one line — can one line sometimes be very great?

2. Is it necessary to know which part is in Valmiki and which part is in the later telling?

3. In the later telling, why did Rama worship before the bridge?

4. Why was Hanuman delayed — can being late sometimes be good?

5. Rama said — your linga will be worshipped first. Was that love for Hanuman — or justice?

6. Why are there two Shiva lingas — one made by Rama, one brought by Hanuman?

7. Rameshwaram is still a living temple — is a story staying alive its greatest truth?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source — One Line in Valmiki

The Valmiki part of this book is only one line — Yuddha Kanda, sarga 123, verse 19. On the way home in the Pushpaka vimana, Rama says to Sita — “This is the shore where Mahadeva formerly bestowed his grace on me.”

The Other Meaning of “Mahadeva”

Some people read “Mahadeva” in this line not as Shiva, but as Sagara, the ocean — the ocean bestowed its grace on Rama. That is another way of reading it — and this book gives both.

What Is Not in Valmiki

In Valmiki's Ramayana there is no story of installing a Shiva linga — no sand linga, no journey of Hanuman to Kailasa, no two lingas. There is also no worship before the building of the bridge in Valmiki. This is stated plainly in this book.

The Later Telling — The Sand Linga

Rama making a Shiva linga of sand on the shore of the sea and worshipping it — this is the tradition told in the Adhyatma Ramayana, the Shiva Purana, the Skanda Purana and the Ramcharitmanas.

The Later Telling — Hanuman's Journey

Hanuman bringing a linga from Kailasa, being delayed, and Rama saying that his linga will be worshipped first — this too is in the later tradition. In some tellings Kashi is named instead of Kailasa — both are named in this book.

The Later Telling — Two Lingas

The tradition of two Shiva lingas at Rameshwaram — Ramanatha and Vishwanatha — and the order of worship, Vishwanatha first and then Ramanatha — is held in living tradition.

Rameshwaram Today

The Ramanathaswamy Temple, on an island on the sea-coast of Tamil Nadu — it is said that this is the shore. This is held by tradition — it is not proven by archaeology. The temple's corridors and sacred tanks are there today.

What Happens Next

Rama's army is camped on Mount Suvela — and Lanka lies before it. The next story — Mount Suvela and Sarama — is in the next book of this series.

The End · · THE END

Here ends the story of Rameshwaram — beginning with one line, growing through the later tellings, reaching the temple of today.

And whenever you stand on the shore of the sea, remember Rama — who said to Sita on his way home that this was the shore where Mahadeva had bestowed his grace on him.

— The End —
